does-a-bonus-change-the-overtime-rate.ht.text:
← back to the calculator

Does a bonus or shift differential change the overtime rate?

Yes, when the bonus is nondiscretionary. It is easy to treat a production bonus or a night-shift differential as extra pay sitting off to the side of the overtime calculation -- but the federal FLSA folds it into the regular rate first, which changes the overtime premium owed on every hour already worked past the threshold that week.

Common questions

Does a bonus change the overtime rate?

Yes, if it is nondiscretionary. Under the federal FLSA, a nondiscretionary bonus (one promised or expected in advance, such as a production, attendance, or quality bonus) is added to the employee's earnings for the period it covers before the regular rate is calculated. A higher regular rate means a higher overtime premium on every hour already worked past the threshold that week -- the bonus does not sit off to the side of the overtime math, it changes it.

What counts as a nondiscretionary bonus?

One the employee could reasonably expect from a formula, quota, or announced policy set in advance -- a production bonus, a perfect-attendance bonus, a shift differential paid for working nights or weekends, a nonexempt commission. A true discretionary bonus (the amount and the fact of paying it are both decided at the employer's sole discretion near the end of the period, with no prior promise or formula) is excluded from the regular rate. Calling a bonus discretionary does not make it so -- a formula or a standing policy makes it nondiscretionary even if the paperwork says otherwise.

How do you fold a bonus into the regular rate by hand?

Add the bonus to the straight-time earnings for the period it covers, then divide by the total hours worked in that same period -- that is the regular rate. The overtime premium is half that regular rate for each hour worked past the threshold, added on top of straight-time pay already paid at the base rate for every hour including the overtime ones. A bonus covering more than one workweek (monthly or quarterly) has to be apportioned back across the workweeks it covers before this step, which is its own calculation this page does not walk through.

Does this calculator include bonuses automatically?

No. The blended-rate calculator on this page computes the regular rate from hours-and-rate rows you enter; it has no separate bonus field, and adding a bonus as a fake extra row would also inflate the total hours the threshold is measured against, producing a wrong total rather than a close one. Compute the bonus-inclusive regular rate by hand with the formula above, then use it to check the total the same way you would check any other overtime figure -- this page is the arithmetic, not a substitute for it.

A worked example

An employee earns $20/hour, works 45 hours in the workweek, and receives a $90 production bonus that covers that single workweek.

StepArithmeticResult
Straight-time pay at the base rate45 hours × $20$900
Add the nondiscretionary bonus$900 + $90$990
Bonus-inclusive regular rate$990 ÷ 45 hours$22 / hour
Overtime premium (half-time) on the 5 hours past 405 × ($22 × 0.5)$55
Total pay for the week$990 + $55$1,045

Compare the $22/hour regular rate above with this employee's own single-rate calculation, which the bonus never touches: without the bonus, the regular rate is the plain $20/hour base rate and the overtime premium on those same 5 hours is only $50, not $55. The $90 bonus is not fully separate pay -- $5 of the premium above exists only because the bonus raised the regular rate it is calculated from.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator apply the federal FLSA weighted-average formula (29 CFR 778.115, and 29 CFR 778.208–778.224 for bonus inclusion) to numbers you supply. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, including whether a specific bonus is discretionary or nondiscretionary under your own pay policy, and for checking your state's overtime rules. OVERTIME PAY CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What's the overtime pay — and what if there were two rates?

Two calculators for the arithmetic a payroll week raises: standard time-and-a-half overtime for one hourly rate, and the FLSA weighted-average (blended rate) method for a workweek where someone worked at two or more different hourly rates — the case people get wrong by hand, because the regular rate used for the overtime premium is neither rate on its own. Both run entirely in this browser.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

Standard overtime (one pay rate)

Enter the hourly rate and hours worked, then click Calculate.

Standard overtime result

Blended rate overtime (two or more pay rates in one week)

Add a row for each distinct hourly rate this employee was paid this workweek, with the hours worked at that rate — for example a warehouse shift at one rate and a front-desk shift at another, or a shift-differential premium tracked as a separate rate.

Add each pay rate and its hours, then click Calculate blended rate.

Blended rate result

Pay rateHoursRatePay

Copies every pay rate and its hours, the blended regular rate, the overtime premium, and the total as plain text to paste into a payroll record or a pay question. The “arithmetic only” note is copied with it.

What this does and doesn't do

Both calculators apply the federal FLSA overtime formulas to the numbers you enter. Neither one knows your state's daily-overtime rule, a double-time threshold, your nondiscretionary bonus structure, or your specific pay policy — those can all change the regular rate or the threshold under FLSA and state law. Treat the output as the arithmetic behind your own payroll record or pay question, not a legal determination of what is owed.

Common questions

How do you calculate overtime pay with one hourly rate?

Pay the hours up to the overtime threshold (40 hours a week under federal FLSA rules) at the regular rate, and pay the hours past the threshold at the overtime rate — the regular rate times the overtime multiplier, 1.5x by default ("time and a half").

How do you calculate overtime when an employee worked at two different pay rates in the same week?

Under the federal FLSA weighted-average method (29 CFR 778.115), the regular rate for that week is total straight-time earnings divided by total hours worked — not either rate on its own, and not a simple average of the two rates. The overtime premium is half that blended rate for each hour worked past the threshold, because straight-time pay for every hour, including the overtime hours, is already counted once in the straight-time total.

Why is the overtime premium only half the blended rate, not 1.5 times it?

Because straight-time pay for every hour worked — including the hours past the overtime threshold — is already included once in the total straight-time pay. Adding the full 1.5x rate for those hours would double-count the first 1x. Adding only the extra 0.5x (the "half-time premium") brings each overtime hour up to time-and-a-half in total.

Does this apply in every state?

This calculator applies the federal FLSA rules: a 40-hour weekly threshold and a 1.5x multiplier by default. Several states require more — daily overtime past a set number of hours in a single day, a double-time threshold, or a higher minimum multiplier — and nondiscretionary bonuses or shift differentials can also change the regular rate. Check your state's rules and your specific pay policy before relying on the total.

Is this legal or payroll advice?

No. This calculator only applies the arithmetic you configure (threshold and multiplier) to the hours and rates you enter — it does not know your state's overtime rules, your bonus structure, or your specific pay policy, and it is not a substitute for reviewing those or consulting a qualified professional.

You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for checking your state's overtime rules and your own pay policy. vs-doing-it-by-hand.html.text:
← back to the calculator

This calculator vs. doing it by hand

Blended-rate overtime is arithmetic anyone can do with a calculator or a spreadsheet. The problem is that the correct method has two non-obvious steps — weighting the regular rate by hours instead of averaging it, and applying only half the blended rate as the overtime premium instead of the full 1.5x — and a hand calculation that misses either one produces a wrong total that still looks reasonable.

Where a hand calculation usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
Finding the regular rate for the weekAverage the two rates (e.g. ($20 + $15) / 2 = $17.50), which ignores how many hours were worked at each.Total straight-time pay ÷ total hours — correctly weighted by hours actually worked at each rate.
Applying the overtime premiumMultiply overtime hours by the full 1.5x blended rate, double-counting the straight-time pay for those hours that is already in the total.Multiplies overtime hours by only the extra half-time premium (0.5x the blended rate), on top of straight-time pay already counted once.
Reusing a rate across weeksCarrying over last week's blended rate or a job title's "usual" rate, which is wrong the moment the hours-at-each-rate mix changes.Recomputes the regular rate fresh from this week's entries every time.
Adding a third rate laterA spreadsheet formula built for two rate columns silently ignores a third row if the SUM range wasn't extended.Add-a-row supports any number of rates; the total always sums every row present.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the most common mistake when calculating blended-rate overtime by hand?

Averaging the two hourly rates instead of weighting by hours. A simple average treats 5 hours at one rate the same as 35 hours at it; the correct regular rate is total straight-time pay divided by total hours, which weights each rate by how much of the week was actually worked at it.

Why does applying the full 1.5x rate to overtime hours overpay every time?

Because the straight-time total already counts every hour worked once, including the overtime hours, at their own rate. Multiplying the overtime hours by the full blended rate again and adding 1.5x on top double-counts that first 1x. The correct premium is only the extra half-time (0.5x the blended rate) on top of straight-time pay that is already there.

Can I just use one employee's usual rate as the "regular rate" for the week?

No, if they worked at more than one rate that week. The FLSA regular rate for a week with multiple hourly rates is specific to that week's mix of hours — it changes whenever the split between rates changes, even for the same employee doing the same two jobs. A rate reused from a previous week or from one job title is not the regular rate for a week with a different mix.

Is a spreadsheet formula good enough once it's built once?

Only if it is built correctly and nobody adds a third rate, changes the threshold, or copies a cell reference wrong later. A formula that hardcodes two rate columns silently produces a wrong total the day a third rate row is added and the SUM range isn't updated — a common way a working sheet quietly breaks weeks after it was checked.

Does this calculator know my state's overtime rules?

No — neither this calculator nor a spreadsheet built from the FAQ here knows your state's daily-overtime, double-time, or bonus-inclusion rules. Both apply the federal FLSA weighted-average formula to the numbers you enter; check your state's rules and your own pay policy before relying on the total.

vs-spreadsheet.html.text:
← back to the calculator

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet

A payroll admin who handles blended-rate overtime more than once usually ends up with a spreadsheet formula for it: sum the straight-time pay, divide by total hours for the regular rate, then add half that rate for each overtime hour. That formula is correct if every cell reference is right and the "half, not the full rate" rule is remembered every time it is copied to a new row.

What each one is for

A spreadsheet can compute this correctly, and many payroll admins already have a formula for it. What it does not do on its own is show the full breakdown for a specific week in a form you can hand to someone else, or stop a copied formula from silently pointing at the wrong row after rates or hours change.

This calculator applies the FLSA weighted-average method (29 CFR 778.115) to the rates and hours you enter, shows the regular rate, the straight-time total, and the overtime premium as separate lines, and lets you copy the full breakdown as a plain-text record -- no formula to write or re-check.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Can I compute blended-rate overtime in a spreadsheet?Yes -- if the formula is right and stays right as rows are added.
Is the overtime premium the full rate or half the rate?Half the blended rate -- the mistake this calculator's FAQ and this page both call out.
Can I hand someone the full breakdown without re-deriving it?This calculator's copy-breakdown output, not a screenshot of a formula bar.
Does either one know my state's overtime rules?Neither -- both apply only the federal threshold and multiplier you configure.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet calculate blended-rate overtime?

Yes, with the right formula: total straight-time earnings divided by total hours gives the regular rate, and the overtime premium is half that regular rate for each overtime hour. The arithmetic itself is not hard — getting every cell reference right, and remembering it is half the rate rather than the full 1.5x, is where a hand-built sheet most often goes wrong.

Why do people apply the full overtime rate to the blended calculation by mistake?

Because that is the right move for a single hourly rate, and the blended-rate case looks similar. It isn't: straight-time pay for every hour worked, including the overtime hours, is already counted once in the total straight-time earnings. Adding the full 1.5x rate on top double-counts that first 1x — only the extra half-time premium is owed.

What does a spreadsheet formula not check for you?

Whether the formula was copied correctly to every row, whether a rate or hours cell was left pointing at last week's numbers, and whether the result actually equals time-and-a-half in total once the premium is added. A calculator built for this one purpose runs the same formula every time and shows the full breakdown so the total is checkable by eye.

Does either one know my state's overtime rules?

No. Both this calculator and a spreadsheet apply only the rules you configure — the federal FLSA 40-hour threshold and 1.5x multiplier by default. Several states require more: daily overtime, a double-time threshold, or a higher minimum multiplier. Check your state's rules and your own pay policy before relying on either total.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator this page links to runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is uploaded.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator apply a published federal formula to numbers you supply; they are not legal, tax, or payroll advice. You are responsible for verifying anything here against your own pay policy and applicable state law. why-overtime-resets-every-workweek.html.text:
← back to the calculator

Why overtime is calculated per workweek, not per pay period

A pay period is a payroll schedule -- weekly, biweekly, semi-monthly, or monthly. Overtime is a per-workweek calculation under the FLSA, a fixed 168-hour period the employer sets, and the two do not have to line up. Summing a biweekly pay period's hours first and applying the 40-hour threshold once to the total is a different calculation than applying the threshold separately to each of the two workweeks inside it, and the two give different answers.

A worked example

An hourly employee at $20/hr works 35 hours in workweek one and 45 hours in workweek two of the same biweekly pay period -- 80 hours total, paid on one check.

MethodRegular hoursOvertime hoursTotal pay
Correct: each workweek calculated separately, then summed35 + 40 = 750 + 5 = 5$700.00 + $950.00 = $1,650.00
Wrong: 80 hours summed first, threshold applied once4040$2,000.00

The wrong method treats the whole 80-hour pay period as if it were a single workweek, so it runs the 40-hour threshold against 80 hours instead of against each week's own hours -- turning 35 straight-time hours in week one into overtime it never was, and overpaying by $350.00 on this one pay period. The direction of the error depends on the split: a week that never crosses 40 hours on its own can still get counted as overtime once it is summed into a period total that does.

Both totals use this calculator's own single-rate function, run once per workweek for the correct total and once against the summed 80 hours for the wrong one -- the only input that changes is which hours are handed to it in a single call.

Common questions

Does overtime reset every pay period, or every workweek?

Every workweek -- a fixed, recurring 168-hour period the employer designates, which does not have to align with the pay period. A biweekly pay period covers two separate workweeks, a semi-monthly period can split a single workweek across two paychecks, and the 40-hour overtime threshold applies once per workweek regardless of how the pay period is drawn around it.

What goes wrong if I sum a biweekly pay period's hours and apply the threshold once?

The 40-hour threshold gets applied to the wrong number. A biweekly employee working 35 hours one week and 45 the next worked 80 hours total, but owes overtime for only the 5 hours past 40 in the second week -- summing first and applying one 40-hour threshold to 80 hours instead produces 40 hours of overtime, vastly overpaying, because it treats a two-week total as if it were a single workweek.

Can a biweekly total ever match the sum of the two workweeks calculated separately?

Only when neither individual workweek crosses the 40-hour threshold on its own, or when both workweeks are calculated separately and then added -- never when the two weeks' hours are added together first and the threshold is applied to that combined total. The two methods agree only in the coincidental case where summing first happens not to push the total over 40 by more than one week's overtime would have produced anyway, which is not something to rely on.

Does this calculator handle a full pay period at once?

No, by design -- it calculates one workweek at a time, which is what the law actually measures. For a biweekly or semi-monthly pay period, run each workweek inside it through the calculator separately and add the results, the same way the worked example on this page does.
